newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - FX volatilities start recoiling in U.S.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - FX volatilities start recoiling in U.S.

text.p: Implied volatilities for dollar-pair options, which had spiked up in recent sessions due to the dollar's relentless slide, started recoiling as spot hovered above Tuesday's lows, U.S. dealers said.

With a long weekend coming up in the United States and Britain, where Monday is a public holiday, time decay began to weigh on everyone's mind, particularly with front-end options priced at very rich volatility levels.
"People aren't as bid for gamma anymore," said Ted Voorhees, a senior trader at Deutsche Bank in New York, referring to the gamma-rich short-dated options.
The volatility curve in most currency pairs had become inverted in recent weeks, most sharply in dollar/yen, as dealers who had negative-gamma positions were forced to bid up the short dates.
But high-gamma options have steeper time decay, and their rich implied volatilities also demand a lot of spot movement to recoup the premium payment through delta-hedge spot trades.

"It's still somewhat volatile but for the most part, outside of dollar/yen, we're in a trading range," Voorhees said. Spot dollar/mark was drifting in a well-traveled area around 1.69 marks in U.S. business.
Implied volatility for one-month dollar/mark options stood at 9.6/9.9 percent in late morning U.S. trade, off a quarter point from late Tuesday levels.
One-month dollar/yen shed nearly a full point to 13.7/14.0 percent. One-week dollar/yen, which had skyrocketed to about 20 percent on Tuesday, was down to 16.0/17.0 percent.
Spot dollar/yen, which plunged to 111.98 yen on Thursday from a May 1 high of 127.47, was meandering in the 114-area.
Still, back-end dollar/yen volatilities were resilient, underpinned by demand for new long-term hedges by end-users and dealers' hedges against their shorts in the front end.
"The dollar's up, but it's still too close for comfort," said one U.S. bank trader. "There's no reason to expect it to stay at these levels."
Six-month and one-year dollar/yen volatilities were 0.1 to 0.2 point easier at 11.3/11.5 and 10.9/11.2 percent respectively.
Traders said risk reversals, which reflect the cost of swapping equally out-of-the-money puts and calls, were shrinking somewhat after being extremely skewed for yen calls in dollar/yen lately.
One-month 25-delta dollar/yen risk reversal was pegged at 1.0/1.3 points in favor of yen calls, off about 0.2 point.

Japanese exporters, who have suddenly become wary about their unhedged dollar revenue streams again after months of absence from the risk reversal market, were likely to reinstate a persistent skew for yen calls, traders said.

Until this year, dollar/yen risk reversals had been constantly favoring yen calls even when the dollar was rising as Japanese corporations actively used the so-called zero-cost options -- tailor-made versions of risk reversals involving yen call buying and yen put selling.
